title: Setting up and compiling
learningGoals: name the three tools you need

youtube.title: C++ Setup on Windows: VS Code and GCC | C++ Programming EP 02
youtube.description: In this episode you will name the three tools you need, compile a file with g++ and run the program you built, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Setting up and compiling · 0:54 A setup check · 1:34 Three tools · 2:04 Second program · 3:10 Recap · 3:42 Bug of the Day · 4:30 Challenge · 4:50 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we set up your computer. You need only three tools. By the end, you build and run a real program.

scenes.onScreen: "Setting up and compiling": numbered lines (1. An editor is where you type code; 2. A compiler builds the program; 3. A terminal runs commands) and an analogy card: a kitchen: the editor is the notebook, the compiler is the stove, the terminal is the table
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: You need three tools. The editor is where you type your code. We use Visual Studio Code. The compiler builds your program. We use g plus plus, from the GCC family. The terminal is where you type commands and run programs. Think of a kitchen. The editor is the notebook with the recipe. The compiler is the stove. The terminal is the table where you eat.
points: An editor is where you type code

analogy.title: Setting up and compiling
analogy.body: A kitchen: the editor is the notebook, the compiler is the stove, the terminal is the table

scenes.onScreen: setup.cpp: a program that prints three ready messages
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: Type this program in your editor and save it as setup dot cpp. [HL 4] The first line of main reports on the editor. [HL 5] The second line reports on the compiler. [HL 6] The third line reports on the terminal. If you see all three lines at the end, your setup works.

code.output:

scenes.onScreen: a table: tool, job and example
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: Look at the table. The editor lets you type and save code. The compiler reads your file and builds a program. The terminal lets you type the compile command and run the result. Every episode uses all three.

diagram.caption: a table: tool, job and example

scenes.onScreen: standard.cpp: a program that prints the language version code
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 4] A built-in name holds a number for the language version. The name starts with two underscores, then c plus plus. With the flag std equals c plus plus twenty, the number is two zero two zero zero two. That number means C plus plus twenty. We use this version in the whole course.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as standard dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. Type g plus plus, then the flags dash std equals c plus plus twenty, dash Wall and dash Wextra. The program prints the version code.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. You need an editor, a compiler and a terminal. Two. The command g plus plus builds your file into a program. Three. The flag dash Wall shows helpful warnings. Four. Always compile again after you change the code. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: You need an editor, a compiler and a terminal.
The command g plus plus builds your file into a program.
The flag dash Wall shows helpful warnings.
Always compile again after you change the code.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A missing include
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Here the include line is missing. The compiler says cout is not a member of std. It even tells you what to do. It asks if you forgot to include iostream. Add the include line at the top, and the error goes away.

scenes.onScreen: Why did the programmer install three tools? Because two was a bug, and four was a feature.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why did the programmer install three tools? Because two was a bug, and four was a feature.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: compile and run setup dot cpp
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Type setup dot cpp, compile it with g plus plus, and run it. Then change one message and compile again. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.onScreen: Next: EP 03 · C vs C++: what changed
scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: what changed from C to C plus plus. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

setup.cpp: In function 'int main()':
setup.cpp:2:10: error: 'cout' is not a member of 'std'
    2 |     std::cout << "Editor: ready" << std::endl;
      |          ^~~~
setup.cpp:1:1: note: 'std::cout' is defined in header '<iostream>'; did you forget to '#include <iostream>'?
  +++ |+#include <iostream>
bug.why: The compiler only knows cout after you include the iostream header. Add the include line at the top of the file.

pun: "Why did the programmer install three tools? Because two was a bug, and four was a feature."
challenge: Type setup dot cpp, compile it with g plus plus, and run it. Then change one message and compile again.
challengeAnswer: Run g plus plus with the file name and dash o setup. Then type dot slash setup. After a change, you must compile again.
